note: ci-speedup is a live-data skill: the measured findings come from sampling a repo's real GitHub Actions run timings via `gh`, so these end-to-end evals require gh auth + network and target public repos. The committed worked examples under reports/ (better-auth, mastra, langfuse) are the recorded expected outputs, and tests/verify_report.py is their invariant gate. The pytest suite under tests/ (test_scan_detectors.py, test_blocking_path.py, test_structural_findings.py, test_collect_runs_sizing.py, test_committed_reports.py, ...) is the primary offline regression eval; these scenarios cover the user-visible end-to-end behaviour. Entries carrying `checks` (6, 10, 11, 12 and 13) run as real agent sessions against an offline replay of the synthetic repo via maintainers/scripts/run_skill_evals.py (see evals/README.md); the rest are manual reference cases, and the no-skill baseline in `baseline` remains unrecorded.
baseline: Model-progress (deprecation) signal — these evals should periodically be run WITHOUT the skill loaded to check whether the base model has caught up (a no-skill baseline that now passes means the skill may be redundant). For ci-speedup this risk is low: the value is capability uplift the model cannot reproduce unaided — deterministic gh run-history sampling, the measured wall-clock critical-path/cluster-floor model, and the 89-pattern detector catalog. Baseline status: NOT yet recorded against a no-skill run; re-check when adopting a new base model.

evals.prompt: Audit the CI of better-auth/better-auth for wall-clock optimization opportunities and produce the report.
evals.expected_output: ci-speedup runs the deterministic pipeline (scan.py + collect_runs.py via run.py, then renders with blocking_path.py). The report's critical-path spine names `prisma-adapter Integration Test` as the slowest gating long pole and drills it to the load-bearing cause (repeated Prisma schema rebuilds / `Total Migration Time`), then a SECOND long pole (the next-biggest lever by impact, e.g. the bimodal `test` vitest job). Each pole ends in a copy-paste agent prompt; no fix is prescribed. Nothing is committed or pushed.
expectations: The skill ran the deterministic scripts (scan.py + collect_runs.py + blocking_path.py), not a hand-graded reading of the workflows.
The report shows TWO long poles: a gate (prisma-adapter Integration Test) and a next-biggest lever, each with an ASCII drill-down.
Each pole ends in a ready-to-paste agent prompt and the report prescribes no fix / no code diff.
Every drilled magnitude is validated by a cross-run check, and the report has no 'no drill-down available' coverage-gap dead-end.
tests/verify_report.py passes on the rendered report.
The skill did not commit, push, or open a pull request.

The closing message to the user is about their CI, not the skill: it opens with the measured result — the biggest lever plus each gating long pole as a plain finding (the check + its measured merge-wait cost + its named root cause) — and asks which pole to fix via a single structured question (the AskUserQuestion tool where available; on an agent without one, one plain message carrying the same numbered options), one option per pole, so the user selects rather than types. The full markdown report is OPT-IN (issue #18): it is NOT written to the working tree or announced with a path by default, though it was still rendered + verify-gated internally on this run; 'Save the full report' is one of the offered options, and picking it copies the already-verified report into the working directory. It does NOT narrate the verification gate / symmetric-pole check / goal self-audit ('all checks passed', 'report is complete / trustworthy'), nor any intermediate step like 'now the internal verification gate', and does NOT editorialize that findings 'ship a prompt' or that the skill 'does not prescribe the fix' (phase 6).

The close's Tier-2 option follows the report: IF the rendered report carries at least one source-backed Runner-minute R-row (or, with zero admitted rows, the Bottom line's 'modeled bill opportunities remain in Also noticed' pointer), the SAME single close question also offers 'Take the bill savings (Tier 2)' — after the pole options on a repo with Tier-1 poles, FIRST on a dead-end repo with none; picking it acts on the Tier-2 rows' agent prompts verbatim from the report (with only the modeled pointer, the Also-noticed bill prompts). If the report renders neither surface, the option is absent. The report's own section order never changes either way.
On the user choosing a pole, the skill takes that pole's agent prompt from the report and acts on it (investigates + applies the fix) rather than only re-offering.

evals.prompt: Where is mastra-ai/mastra's CI slow, and what's the second-biggest lever after the worst one?
evals.expected_output: mastra's branch protection resolves a real required set (`Lint`, `Lint docs`, `Unit and E2E Tests / Merge Test Reports`), so the critical-path spine is scoped by `needs:`-reachability to the MERGE-BLOCKING work. Checks that gate no merge are DROPPED from the critical path (recorded in `dropped_non_required_checks` and surfaced as a 'Narrowed to merge-blocking checks' footnote): the non-required `changed-tests` (its own `changed-test-gate.yml`) AND `Validate build outputs` (a `lint.yml` job the required `Lint` does not `needs:`) — neither headlines `why is the merge slow?`, since speeding them moves zero time-to-merge. The gate is `Build` (`prebuild.yml`), which the required `Unit and E2E Tests / Merge Test Reports` reusable invocation transitively `needs:`; it drills DETERMINISTICALLY as `turbo-partial-cache` (caching ON but ~80% of the 152 packages rebuilt every run = cache-key churn). The second long pole is `Unit and E2E Tests / UNIT Test (Shard 4)` (a reusable child of that required rollup), a vitest leg whose dominant cost is importing the module graph: named as the OPT78 per-file-isolation lever (HIGH risk) when mastra's vitest config confirms isolation is still on, otherwise the same measured import-bound split with OPT78 withheld and the reason stated. Both carry a cross-run check; neither is a dead-end.
expectations: With required_checks resolved non-empty and complete, the spine is restricted by needs-reachability to required checks plus the jobs the required work transitively `needs:`; non-required, non-reachable checks (`changed-tests`, `Validate build outputs`) are dropped (in `dropped_non_required_checks`) and NOT headlined, even when one is the slowest check overall.
The drop is visible: a 'Narrowed to merge-blocking checks' footnote names the excluded non-required checks (never a silent drop).

The gate long pole is a merge-blocking check (`Build`, prebuild.yml — the required reusable invocation needs it), drilled via the turbo-partial-cache detector (rebuilt-despite-caching %), NOT a coverage-gap dead-end.

The second long pole (`Unit and E2E Tests / UNIT Test (Shard 4)`, a reusable child of the required Merge Test Reports rollup) drills to its dominant step; matrix legs collapse to one pole (sibling shards are not double-counted).
Both poles carry a cross-run check and end in an agent prompt; no fix is prescribed; nothing is committed or pushed.

evals.prompt: Run a speed audit of langfuse/langfuse's CI and explain the critical path.
evals.expected_output: The single slowest check overall is the managed `Claude Code Review` bot, which has no editable workflow file — the report notes this and makes the slowest FIXABLE check (`tests-web`, a matrix vitest job) the headline pole, plus a second pole (`e2e-tests`). The e2e-tests pole's dominant step is a `turbo run build`; it drills deterministically as turbo-remote-cache (or, on a stack the catalog can't parse, the LLM gap-fill writes a log-grounded analysis) — never a 'no drill-down available' dead-end.
expectations: The report identifies the managed Claude Code Review check as the slowest overall but unfixable (no workflow file), and headlines the slowest fixable check instead.
Two poles live in the same workflow (pipeline.yml) and are correctly disambiguated (matrix tests-web collapses to one; e2e-tests is a distinct pole).
The e2e-tests pole is a complete finding (a deterministic drill or a labelled, log-grounded LLM gap-fill) with a cross-run check — no coverage-gap dead-end.
Each pole ends in an agent prompt; nothing is committed or pushed.

The agent acts on run.py's printed data-pass summary rather than re-deriving: it does NOT re-probe gh for branch protection / rulesets (gating is already resolved into required_checks), does NOT manually investigate the fileless Claude Code Review check's gating (the summary flags it as auto-demoted), and runs the summary's pre-filled render command instead of reading blocking_path.py source to reconstruct the --log/--steps/--mag KEY=PATH bindings.

tests/verify_report.py's 'drills every gating pole' check FAILS on a variant where the second pole is dropped or stripped of the first pole's sections, and PASSES the committed worked examples.

evals.expected_output: With no repo named, ci-speedup defaults to the repo the user is running it in: it resolves the current checkout (git toplevel for the root + `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner` for owner/repo), shows the detected target, and asks the user to confirm it OR supply a different local path / owner-repo BEFORE running any scan or gh data pass. evals.prompt: Audit a mature repo whose merge gate is already tight, but whose Actions history contains superseded runs that waste runner-minutes.
evals.expected_output: Tier 1 remains first and wall-clock-scoped. When the findings JSON contains measured, certified Tier-2 findings, the report renders `Runner-minute reductions (wall-clock-neutral)` after Pre-start wait and before Also noticed. R-rows are ranked by billable-equivalent runner minutes, carry the measured evidence and a machine-derived neutrality proof, and verify_report fails if a corrupted certificate, modeled sizing, or total is rendered. The run.py stdout summary also includes a Tier 2 line with the neutral count, raw credited minutes per month, and the top promoted pattern/workflow.
evals.note: Regression eval for the runner-minutes Tier-2 shape added in the PR-3/PR-4 sequence. It asserts the section contract and stdout handoff, not a specific repo's numbers.
expectations: The report order is still wall-clock-first: long poles, Pre-start wait, Runner-minute reductions, then Also noticed.
Only findings with `sizing_basis="measured"` and a `tier2_neutrality` certificate render as R-numbered Tier-2 rows; modeled or uncertified runner-minute findings stay residual.
Every R-row carries measured evidence and a neutrality line backed by a typed `runner_minutes` claim.
tests/verify_report.py fails variants that tamper with the Tier-2 certificate, measured basis, de-overlapped total, or top-finding claim binding.
The agent-facing data-pass summary prints the Tier 2 count, raw credited runner-minutes/month, and top promoted pattern/workflow so the agent does not re-derive those facts by hand.

evals.prompt: Audit a repo whose slowest gating check is a large matrix test job, then act on the pole's agent prompt as the downstream coding agent.
evals.expected_output: Every hand-off ci-speedup emits - the catalog prompt, the generic no-catalog prompt, the no-job-timing variant, the LLM gap-fill prompt, and each hygiene / Tier-2 / queue-wait prompt - carries the same no-weakening rail: speed is never bought by reducing what CI verifies. A downstream agent that proposes deleting or narrowing matrix legs, adding `continue-on-error` / `|| true` / any other exit-code suppression, narrowing or removing a required status check (or changing a job so a required check stops reporting), skipping tests that cover the change behind a path/branch filter, or cutting test counts, timeouts, or retries to weaken the signal rather than the cost is refused by its own prompt and says so instead of shipping. Two exceptions are stated: a reduction the RCA itself named as the measured finding, and a conditional skip of a check the change cannot fail on - a `paths`/`paths-ignore` filter, a draft or job-level `if:`, changed-scope selection - which is what the catalog's own fix recipe for the skip-family patterns prescribes, so long as the commit that merges is still verified by the full set.
evals.note: Regression eval for the no-weakening rail. The fastest CI is one that tests nothing, and every forbidden shape above scores as a win in the very wall-clock numbers ci-speedup measures - so the rail lives in the prompt, which is the whole contract with the downstream agent. Asserts the hand-off's CONTENT, not a repo's numbers; tests/test_no_weakening_rail.py is the executable gate.
expectations: Every rendered `Prompt for your coding agent` block contains the no-weakening rail, on every prompt path (catalog match, no catalog match, no job timing, LLM gap-fill, hygiene / Tier-2 / queue-wait).

The rail names each forbidden edit explicitly: deleted or narrowed matrix legs, `continue-on-error` / `|| true` / other exit-code suppression, a narrowed or removed required status check or a job changed so a required check stops reporting, tests that cover the change skipped behind a path/branch filter, and reduced test counts / timeouts / retries that weaken the signal rather than the cost.

The rail does not forbid the skill's own fix recipes: not running a check against a change it cannot fail on is not checking less, so a `paths`/`paths-ignore` filter, a draft or job-level `if:`, or changed-scope test selection stays in bounds while the commit that merges is still verified by the full set. A prompt that links a catalog recipe and then forbids it is a defect.
The rail is an exception rule, not a blanket ban: a reduction the RCA itself named as the measured finding stays fixable.
A downstream agent handed the prompt refuses a coverage-reducing edit and reports that it stopped, rather than delivering a faster pipeline that checks less.
The rail does not add a second copy of the load-bearing `does NOT prescribe the fix` disclaimer, so verify_report's one-disclaimer-per-prompt invariant still holds.

evals.prompt: Audit a pnpm monorepo whose slowest gating check is a 162s lint job; its step "Run lint and format checks" takes 52s and runs `pnpm lint`, which package.json resolves to `eslint . && prettier --check .`. Then audit a second repo whose format step already runs `oxfmt --check`.
evals.expected_output: On the first repo, the lint pole carries one OPT84 card (a slow step on the long pole runs a tool that has a native drop-in), inside the pole's section. It names the step, its measured 52s p50 (32% of the 162s job), the resolved command through package.json, and both tools: ESLint → oxlint (the card's fit reads `drop-in` only when the config was read in full and shows nothing oxlint lacks; `run both: …` with the stamped reasons when the config has custom local rules, a plugin oxlint does not carry natively or type-aware rules; `see OPT82 first` when OPT82 already reports the step; and risk HIGH on the card whenever it reports the ESLint row, drop-in or run both) and Prettier → oxfmt (`drop-in`, or `run both: …` when a Prettier plugin is declared), each with the target's migration docs and overview docs and the catalog's published range labelled as the catalog's, not the repo's. The only number for the repo is the 52s ceiling, stated as the most the swaps can remove, not a forecast, with a sentence that how it splits between the two tools is unknown until measured. No wall-clock or runner-minute saving is credited, and nothing reaches the headline, Tier 2, Also noticed or any total. On the second repo, OPT84 stays silent on Prettier: the step already runs the target.
evals.note: Regression eval for OPT84 (uncredited, routed from the drilled pole, like OPT83). Asserts the card's shape and the uncredited contract, not a specific repo's numbers; the lint pole is a synthetic shape (a live run on mastra is silent, because its packages already run oxlint and its root runs oxfmt), and mastodon's oxfmt format check is the real-repo shape behind the second repo's silence.
expectations: Exactly one OPT84 card renders for the lint pole, in that pole's section, naming both ESLint → oxlint and Prettier → oxfmt.

The card's only repo-measured durations are the step's 52s p50 and the job's 162s, with the 52s presented as a ceiling, never as a saving; the finding carries `sizing_basis` uncredited and no `wall_clock_p50_s` or `runner_min_saving`.
Each tool row's fit uses the card's own words (`drop-in`, `run both: …` or `see OPT82 first`), never "partial fit" or "mostly drop-in".

The card links each target's own migration docs, says to benchmark both tools on the same commit and runner class before claiming a number, and carries the no-weakening rail (no rule, plugin, file set or check is dropped; dual-run when the target lacks one).
No OPT84 number is summed into the headline, Tier 2, Also noticed or any total.
On a repo whose format step already runs `oxfmt --check`, no OPT84 card mentions Prettier.

evals.name: gap-fill-coverage-lookup
evals.prompt:
I'm about to write a ci-speedup phase-4a gap-fill for a long pole of our repo, `tests.yml` > `test (3.14)`, which the report rendered with no drill-down. Its dominant step is `Install dependencies` (6m 51s of an 8m 37s job). The relevant part of that step's log:

```
2026-10-20T09:12:04.1180000Z Collecting numpy==2.1.3
2026-10-20T09:12:04.9020000Z   Downloading numpy-2.1.3.tar.gz (20.2 MB)
2026-10-20T09:12:07.3310000Z   Installing build dependencies: started
2026-10-20T09:12:19.7740000Z Building wheels for collected packages: numpy
2026-10-20T09:12:19.7750000Z   Building wheel for numpy (pyproject.toml): started
2026-10-20T09:18:41.2260000Z   Building wheel for numpy (pyproject.toml): finished with status 'done'
2026-10-20T09:18:41.3010000Z Successfully built numpy
```

The 3.12 and 3.13 legs of the same matrix install in under 40s. Before I write the analysis, use the ci-speedup skill to check: does its pattern catalog already describe this cause? Look it up, don't guess. End your reply with one line `CATALOG-PATTERN: OPT<n>` or `CATALOG-PATTERN: none`.
evals.expected_output: The agent looks the stack up in the ci-speedup pattern catalog and finds OPT86 (CI compiles a dependency that ships prebuilt): a manual pattern no detector emits, whose heuristic is exactly a `Building wheel for <pkg>` span on one matrix leg. It answers `CATALOG-PATTERN: OPT86`.
evals.note: Reading-sensitive: the corpus has no coverage-gap pole, so this asks the coverage question a gap-fill must answer first. OPT86 is a manual pattern (no detector, no script names it beside a log shape), so the id is only found in the catalog. Reading is recorded, not capped: the bound is set from the committed baseline.
expectations: The agent consults the pattern catalog rather than answering from memory.
The final line names OPT86.

evals.name: no-catalog-read-needed
evals.prompt: Run a CI speed audit of synthetic/repo (the git checkout in the current directory) and tell me just two things: how long a typical pull request waits for its CI checks, and which check's job is the slowest. Just the numbers, I don't need fixes.
evals.expected_output: ci-speedup runs its data pass on the replayed history, renders and verifies the report, and answers with the measured headline: a typical PR waits 3m 40s, and `CI / test` is the slowest single job at a 3m 17s median. Nothing in the question needs the pattern catalog.
evals.note: Reading-sensitive control: whether the catalog is opened is recorded per run and deliberately NOT asserted in the baseline; the split refactor is expected to drive it to zero. Graded on the answer, not the report file: the runner only collects a report at a literal absolute path, and agents often write it under a shell variable.
expectations: The audit runs its data pass.
The answer states the 3m 40s typical wait and names `CI / test` as the slowest job.
